claim: Cool ambient temperatures are major cues determining flowering time in spring.
source: Cool ambient temperatures are major cues determining flowering time in spring.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, FLOWERING LOCUS M (FLM) regulates flowering in the ambient temperature range.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, FLOWERING LOCUS M (FLM) regulates flowering in the ambient temperature range and FLM is transcribed and alternatively spliced in a temperature-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, likely supported by prior literature.

claim: FLM is transcribed and alternatively spliced in a temperature-dependent manner.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, FLOWERING LOCUS M (FLM) regulates flowering in the ambient temperature range and FLM is transcribed and alternatively spliced in a temperature-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, likely supported by prior literature.

claim: Polymorphic promoter and intronic sequences are required for FLM expression and splicing.
source: We identify polymorphic promoter and intronic sequences required for FLM expression and splicing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transgenic experiments covered 69% of the available sequence variation in two distinct sites.
source: In transgenic experiments covering 69% of the available sequence variation in two distinct sites, we show that variation in the abundance of the FLM-ß splice form strictly correlate (R2 = 0.94) with flowering time over an extended vegetative period.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: Variation in the abundance of the FLM-ß splice form strictly correlates (R2 = 0.94) with flowering time over an extended vegetative period.
source: In transgenic experiments covering 69% of the available sequence variation in two distinct sites, we show that variation in the abundance of the FLM-ß splice form strictly correlate (R2 = 0.94) with flowering time over an extended vegetative period.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: FLM polymorphisms lead to changes in FLM expression (PRO2+).
source: The FLM polymorphisms lead to changes in FLM expression (PRO2+) but may also affect FLM intron 1 splicing (INT6+).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: FLM polymorphisms may affect FLM intron 1 splicing (INT6+).
source: The FLM polymorphisms lead to changes in FLM expression (PRO2+) but may also affect FLM intron 1 splicing (INT6+).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data, with some speculative element indicated by 'may'.

claim: Temperature is one major cue controlling flowering time, particularly before the winter but also during spring when ambient cool temperatures generally delay and warm temperatures promote flowering.
source: Temperature is one major cue controlling flowering time, particularly before the winter but also during spring when ambient cool temperatures generally delay and warm temperatures promote flowering.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Different molecular pathways controlling flowering in different temperature ranges and environments have been genetically dissected.
source: Different molecular pathways controlling flowering in different temperature ranges and environments have been genetically dissected (Capovilla et al., 2015; Verhage et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In many plant species and in many accessions of Arabidopsis thaliana, the vernalization pathway prevents premature flowering before the long cold periods of the winter.
source: In many plant species and in many accessions of the plant model species Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis), the well-studied vernalization pathway prevents premature flowering before the long cold periods of the winter (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Flowering of winter-annual Arabidopsis accessions without vernalization is strongly delayed by the MADS-box transcription factor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC).
source: In Arabidopsis, flowering of winter-annual accessions without vernalization is strongly delayed by the MADS-box transcription factor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) (Song et al., 2012; Michaels and Amasino, 1999, 2001; Johanson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: FLC forms a repressor complex through interactions with the MADS-box transcription factor SVP (SHORT VEGETATIVE PHASE) to repress the transcription of the flowering promoting genes FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) and SUPPRESSOR OF OVEREXPRESSION OF CO1 (SOC1).
source: FLC forms a repressor complex through interactions with the MADS-box transcription factor SVP (SHORT VEGETATIVE PHASE) to repress the transcription of the flowering promoting genes FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) and SUPPRESSOR OF OVEREXPRESSION OF CO1 (SOC1) (Li et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: As a result of the prolonged exposure to cold temperatures during winter, FLC abundance is gradually reduced, predominantly through epigenetic mechanisms, and flowering repression is gradually relieved.
source: As a result of the prolonged exposure to cold temperatures during winter, FLC abundance is gradually reduced, predominantly through epigenetic mechanisms, and flowering repression is gradually relieved (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Substantial natural variation in the vernalization-dependent expression of FLC has been described and characterized in many Arabidopsis accessions.
source: Substantial natural variation in the vernalization-dependent expression of FLC has already been described and characterized in many Arabidopsis accessions (Coustham et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Temperature changes by only a few degree Celsius during cold or warm spring periods shift flowering time in many plant species.
source: Temperature changes by only a few degree Celsius (°C) during cold or warm spring periods shift flowering time in many plant species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Temperature changes associated with global warming could lead to flowering changes and threaten agricultural production systems.
source: Since temperature changes associated with global warming could lead to similar flowering changes and threaten agricultural production systems, elucidating the ambient temperature pathway has recently received increased attention (Moore and Lobell, 2015; Wheeler and von Braun, 2013; Jagadish et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a speculative concern about future impacts.

claim: After vernalization or in vernalization-insensitive accessions, flowering in ambient temperatures is largely under control of the FLC-related FLOWERING LOCUS M (FLM) and residual FLC retains only a minor role.
source: After vernalization or in vernalization-insensitive accessions, flowering in ambient temperatures is largely under control of the FLC-related FLOWERING LOCUS M (FLM) and residual FLC retains only a minor role (Gu et al., 2013; Balasubramanian et al., 2006; Blázquez et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FLM controls flowering in the range between 5°C and 23°C.
source: FLM controls flowering in the range between 5°C and 23°C and FLM can form, just like FLC, a flowering repressive complex with SVP (Lee et al., 2013; Posé et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FLM can form, just like FLC, a flowering repressive complex with SVP.
source: FLM controls flowering in the range between 5°C and 23°C and FLM can form, just like FLC, a flowering repressive complex with SVP (Lee et al., 2013; Posé et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Besides FLM, as the dominant regulator, ambient temperature flowering is also regulated by the FLM-homologs MAF2 - MAF4.
source: Besides FLM, as the dominant regulator, ambient temperature flowering is also regulated by the FLM-homologs MAF2 - MAF4 (Li et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013; Ratcliffe et al., 2003; Airoldi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of SVP lead to early and temperature-insensitive flowering in the range between 5°C and 27°C.
source: Conversely, loss-of-function mutations of SVP lead to early and temperature-insensitive flowering in the range between 5°C and 27°C (Lee et al., 2007, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Within the ambient temperature range, FLM is differentially spliced in a temperature-dependent manner through the alternative use of the exons 2 (FLM-ß) and 3 (FLM-δ).
source: Within the ambient temperature range, FLM is differentially spliced in a temperature-dependent manner through the alternative use of the exons 2 (FLM-ß) and 3 (FLM-δ).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, likely supported by prior literature.

claim: Based on transgenic experiments, a model was proposed according to which FLM-ß and FLM-δ function antagonistically with SVP.
source: Based on transgenic experiments, a model was proposed according to which FLM-ß and FLM-δ function antagonistically with SVP.
evidence: This is a description of a prior model from the literature.

claim: According to a prior model, FLM-ß engages in flowering repressive interactions with SVP in cooler temperatures.
source: Accordingly, FLM-ß engages in flowering repressive interactions with SVP in cooler temperatures.
evidence: This is a description of a prior model from the literature.

claim: According to a prior model, FLM-δ would outcompete FLM-ß in warmer temperatures and form heterodimers with SVP unable to bind DNA and repress flowering.
source: Conversely, FLM-δ would outcompete FLM-ß in warmer temperatures and form heterodimers with SVP unable to bind DNA and repress flowering (Lee et al., 2013; Posé et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of a prior model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Recent data suggest that the model proposing antagonistic function of FLM-ß and FLM-δ may not be valid in natural contexts.
source: Recent data suggest that this attractive model, based solely on transgenic experiments, may not be valid in natural contexts (Sureshkumar et al., 2016; Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Two FLM deletion alleles conferring temperature-insensitive early flowering were identified in the Arabidopsis accessions Niederzenz-1 (Nd-1) and Eifel-6 (Ei-6).
source: Although two FLM deletion alleles conferring temperature-insensitive early flowering were identified in the Arabidopsis accessions Niederzenz-1 (Nd-1) and Eifel-6 (Ei-6), their limited demographic and genetic spread indicated that FLM deletions may be disadvantageous (Werner et al., 2005; Balasubramanian and Weigel, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The limited demographic and genetic spread of FLM deletion alleles indicated that FLM deletions may be disadvantageous.
source: Although two FLM deletion alleles conferring temperature-insensitive early flowering were identified in the Arabidopsis accessions Niederzenz-1 (Nd-1) and Eifel-6 (Ei-6), their limited demographic and genetic spread indicated that FLM deletions may be disadvantageous (Werner et al., 2005; Balasubramanian and Weigel, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations cited from prior literature.

claim: A first FLM expression variant was determined from the early flowering accession Killian-0 (Kil-0).
source: A first FLM expression variant was determined from the early flowering accession Killian-0 (Kil-0).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding, likely from the authors' previous work.

claim: In Kil-0, a LINE retrotransposon insertion in FLM intron 1 caused premature transcription termination, aberrant FLM splicing, consequently reduced FLM expression and earlier flowering.
source: In Kil-0, a LINE retrotransposon insertion in FLM intron 1 caused premature transcription termination, aberrant FLM splicing, consequently reduced FLM expression and earlier flowering.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding, likely from the authors' previous work.

claim: The Kil-0 phenotype was especially prominent at a temperature of 15°C, which is closer to the average temperature in the native range of the species than the commonly used 21°C.
source: This phenotype was especially prominent at a temperature of 15°C , which is closer to the average temperature in the native range of the species than the commonly used 21°C (Lutz et al., 2015; Hoffmann, 2002; Weigel, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The identification of nine further accessions with an identical LINE insertion was suggestive for a recent adaptive selective sweep.
source: The subsequent identification of nine further accessions with an identical LINE insertion was suggestive for a recent adaptive selective sweep (Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on data cited from prior literature.

claim: FLM expression-modulating alleles are advantageous for flowering time adaptation in the ambient temperature range.
source: It was thus concluded that FLM expression-modulating alleles are advantageous for flowering time adaptation in the ambient temperature range, particularly since there are no other pleiotropic growth changes observed in FLM mutant alleles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from prior observations and inferences.

claim: There are no other pleiotropic growth changes observed in FLM mutant alleles.
source: It was thus concluded that FLM expression-modulating alleles are advantageous for flowering time adaptation in the ambient temperature range, particularly since there are no other pleiotropic growth changes observed in FLM mutant alleles.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior work.

claim: An intronless FLM cDNA expressed from a FLM promoter fragment was unable to rescue the flm mutant phenotype.
source: Previous work had shown that an intronless FLM cDNA expressed from a FLM promoter fragment was unable to rescue the flm mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding from previous work.

claim: Important information for FLM expression may reside in FLM non-coding sequences.
source: Since this suggested that important information for FLM expression may reside in FLM non-coding sequences, we examined non-coding sequence polymorphisms with a potential role in controlling FLM expression and splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior observations that motivated the current study.

claim: Using phylogenetic footprinting, conserved FLM promoter and intron 1 regions essential for FLM expression were found.
source: Using phylogenetic footprinting, we found conserved FLM promoter and intron 1 regions essential for FLM expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: By association analysis using polymorphism data from ≈800 Arabidopsis accessions, a small polymorphic region in the FLM promoter and a highly polymorphic nucleotide triplet in FLM intron 6 controlling basal and temperature-dependent FLM expression were identified.
source: By association analysis using polymorphism data from ≈800 Arabidopsis accessions, we identified a small polymorphic region in the FLM promoter and a highly polymorphic nucleotide triplet in FLM intron 6 controlling basal and temperature-dependent FLM expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Small changes in the relative abundance of the FLM-ß splice variant dynamically modulated flowering at 15°C over a range of 15 leaves.
source: Small changes in the relative abundance of the FLM-ß splice variant dynamically modulated flowering at 15°C over a range of 15 leaves.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: When tested in a homogenous genetic background, FLM abundance correlated almost perfectly with flowering time (R2 = 0.94).
source: When tested in a homogenous genetic background, FLM abundance correlated almost perfectly with flowering time (R2 = 0.94) and contributed (R2 = 0.21) to flowering time variation in heterogeneous natural Arabidopsis populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: FLM abundance contributed (R2 = 0.21) to flowering time variation in heterogeneous natural Arabidopsis populations.
source: When tested in a homogenous genetic background, FLM abundance correlated almost perfectly with flowering time (R2 = 0.94) and contributed (R2 = 0.21) to flowering time variation in heterogeneous natural Arabidopsis populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: FLM-ß is an important determinant of flowering during cool or warm spring periods.
source: Our data suggest that FLM-ß is an important determinant of flowering during cool or warm spring periods.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Arabidopsis transgenic lines expressing an intronless FLM from a functional FLM promoter fragment cannot express FLM to detectable levels and fail to rescue the flowering time phenotype of a flm-3 loss-of-function mutant.
source: We previously found that Arabidopsis transgenic lines expressing an intronless FLM from a functional FLM promoter fragment cannot express FLM to detectable levels and fail to rescue the flowering time phenotype of a flm-3 loss-of-function mutant (Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding from the authors' previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: The presence of intron 1 was sufficient to restore the basal expression of FLM at the ambient temperatures 15°C, 21°C, and 27°C.
source: The presence of intron 1 was sufficient to restore the basal expression of FLM at the ambient temperatures 15°C, 21°C, and 27°C, but introns 2–6 were required for the temperature-sensitive regulation of the splice variants FLM-ß and FLM-δ (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Introns 2–6 were required for the temperature-sensitive regulation of the splice variants FLM-ß and FLM-δ.
source: The presence of intron 1 was sufficient to restore the basal expression of FLM at the ambient temperatures 15°C, 21°C, and 27°C, but introns 2–6 were required for the temperature-sensitive regulation of the splice variants FLM-ß and FLM-δ (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Intron 1 may contain critical information for FLM expression.
source: We concluded that intron 1 may contain critical information for FLM expression and introns 2–6 may contribute to temperature-dependent FLM expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Introns 2–6 may contribute to temperature-dependent FLM expression.
source: We concluded that intron 1 may contain critical information for FLM expression and introns 2–6 may contribute to temperature-dependent FLM expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: One promoter region of 250 bp and two intron 1 regions of 373 and 101 bp with increased sequence conservation (>60%) were detected within the non-coding sequences.
source: Within the non-coding sequences, we detected one promoter region of 250 bp and two intron 1 regions of 373 and 101 bp with increased sequence conservation (>60%) (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic footprinting analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A strong downregulation of FLM at 15°C and 23°C was detected in PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp lines.
source: While we detected a strong downregulation of FLM at 15°C and 23°C in PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp lines, the deletion in INT1Δ101bp had comparably minor effects on FLM expression (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The deletion in INT1Δ101bp had comparably minor effects on FLM expression.
source: While we detected a strong downregulation of FLM at 15°C and 23°C in PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp lines, the deletion in INT1Δ101bp had comparably minor effects on FLM expression (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The proximal 225 bp promoter and the 337 bp intron 1 regions contained important sequences for basal FLM expression.
source: This indicated that the proximal 225 bp promoter and the 337 bp intron 1 regions contained important sequences for basal FLM expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The 254 bp promoter fragment alone was not sufficient to confer FLM expression of a genomic FLM fragment.
source: Subsequent experiments showed that the 254 bp promoter fragment alone was, however, not sufficient to confer FLM expression of a genomic FLM fragment (PRO254bp; Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: 45 promoter and intronic SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF)≥5% were identified in 776 sequenced Arabidopsis accessions.
source: We identified 45 promoter and intronic SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF)≥5% and used these to define ten major haplotypes (H1–-H10) representing 379 (49%) accessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis.

claim: Ten major haplotypes (H1–-H10) representing 379 (49%) accessions were defined using 45 promoter and intronic SNPs.
source: We identified 45 promoter and intronic SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF)≥5% and used these to define ten major haplotypes (H1–-H10) representing 379 (49%) accessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis.

claim: FLM-ß expression decreased (on average 0.6 fold) and FLM-δ increased (on average 1.4 fold) with increasing temperature in most accessions.
source: In line with the reported behaviour of FLM in Col-0, we observed that FLM-ß expression decreased (on average 0.6 fold) and FLM-δ increased (on average 1.4 fold) with increasing temperature in most accessions (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3) (Lee et al., 2013; Posé et al., 2013; Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Substantial variation in FLM-ß and FLM-δ expression was observed between the accessions of the FLM haplotype set.
source: At the same time, we also observed substantial variation in FLM-ß and FLM-δ expression between the accessions of the FLM haplotype set, inviting the conclusion that non-coding sequence variation modulates FLM expression (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Non-coding sequence variation modulates FLM expression.
source: At the same time, we also observed substantial variation in FLM-ß and FLM-δ expression between the accessions of the FLM haplotype set, inviting the conclusion that non-coding sequence variation modulates FLM expression (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Total FLM transcript levels strongly correlated with FLM-ß but not with FLM-δ abundance at 15°C and at 23°C.
source: Since total FLM transcript levels strongly correlated with FLM-ß but not with FLM-δ abundance at 15°C and at 23°C, it could be suggested that FLM-ß represents the major FLM form among the FLM transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: FLM-ß represents the major FLM form among the FLM transcripts.
source: Since total FLM transcript levels strongly correlated with FLM-ß but not with FLM-δ abundance at 15°C and at 23°C, it could be suggested that FLM-ß represents the major FLM form among the FLM transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The PRO2+ and INT6+ sites were directly flanked or in close proximity to a total of four PolyA motifs of variable length ([A]7-11).
source: Strikingly, the PRO2 and INT6 sites were directly flanked or in close proximity to a total of four PolyA motifs of variable length ([A]7-11), one of which represented a so-called CArG-box, a potential binding site for MADS-box transcription factors (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis.

claim: One of the PolyA motifs near PRO2 and INT6 sites represented a so-called CArG-box, a potential binding site for MADS-box transcription factors.
source: Strikingly, the PRO2 and INT6 sites were directly flanked or in close proximity to a total of four PolyA motifs of variable length ([A]7-11), one of which represented a so-called CArG-box, a potential binding site for MADS-box transcription factors (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Two more PolyA motifs resided in introns 3 and 5.
source: Two more PolyA motifs resided in introns 3 and 5 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PolyA motifs had been reported to be important for gene expression.
source: Since PolyA motifs had been reported to be important for gene expression, we reasoned that these motifs could be relevant for FLM regulation, in isolation or in combination with the highly significant non-coding variations (O'Malley et al., 2016; Horton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The PRO1 1 bp deletion, as present in the FLMCol-0 reference, did not reveal differences in FLM transcript levels when compared to PRO1T (FLMCol-0).
source: The PRO1- deletion, as present in the FLMCol-0 reference, did not reveal differences in FLM transcript levels when compared to PRO1T (FLMCol-0) (Fig. Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Two PRO2+ variants (PRO2+GGAAC, PRO2+AAACC) and three INT6+ variants (INT6+ACA, INT6+CAC and INT6+AAA) displayed an upregulation of FLM-ß at 15°C when compared to FLMCol-0.
source: However, two PRO2+ (PRO2+GGAAC, PRO2+AAACC) and three INT6+ variants (INT6+ACA, INT6+CAC and INT6+AAA) displayed an upregulation of FLM-ß at 15°C when compared to FLMCol-0 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Increases and decreases of FLM-δ levels largely followed those of FLM-ß levels except for INT6+AAA, which showed an upregulation exclusively of FLM-ß.
source: Increases and decreases of FLM-δ levels largely followed those of FLM-ß levels except for INT6+AAA, which showed an upregulation exclusively of FLM-ß (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The deletion variant PRO2+Δ16bp showed upregulation of FLM-ß.
source: The deletion variant PRO2+Δ16bp showed upregulation of FLM-ß but INT6+Δ17bp did not have significantly altered FLM-ß and FLM-δ levels when compared to FLMCol-0 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: INT6+Δ17bp did not have significantly altered FLM-ß and FLM-δ levels when compared to FLMCol-0.
source: The deletion variant PRO2+Δ16bp showed upregulation of FLM-ß but INT6+Δ17bp did not have significantly altered FLM-ß and FLM-δ levels when compared to FLMCol-0 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The identity of the PRO2+ and INT6+ regions rather than their presence controlled FLM expression and temperature-sensitive FLM regulation.
source: We concluded that the identity of these regions rather than their presence controlled FLM expression and temperature-sensitive FLM regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The PolyA motif deletion variants showed gradually decreasing FLM-ß and FLM-δ levels with an increasing number of deletions.
source: The PolyA motif deletion variants showed gradually decreasing FLM-ß and FLM-δ levels with an increasing number of deletions while the deletion of all six PolyA motifs (PolyA_6xΔ) had an especially strong effect on FLM-ß expression and its temperature-sensitive expression (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The deletion of all six PolyA motifs (PolyA_6xΔ) had an especially strong effect on FLM-ß expression and its temperature-sensitive expression.
source: The PolyA motif deletion variants showed gradually decreasing FLM-ß and FLM-δ levels with an increasing number of deletions while the deletion of all six PolyA motifs (PolyA_6xΔ) had an especially strong effect on FLM-ß expression and its temperature-sensitive expression (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The PolyA motifs possess a regulatory role but may function in a redundant manner.
source: Thus, the PolyA motifs possess a regulatory role but may function in a redundant manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: A very strong correlation between FLM-ß transcript levels and flowering time (R2 = 0.94) was detected in plants grown at 15°C.
source: We detected a very strong correlation between FLM-ß transcript levels and flowering time (R2 = 0.94) in plants grown at 15°C.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Flowering time responded in a linear manner to FLM-ß levels with 17 to 30 rosette leaves until flowering in the range of relative transcript levels from 0.6 to 2.4.
source: Flowering time responded in a linear manner to FLM-ß levels with 17 to 30 rosette leaves until flowering in the range of relative transcript levels from 0.6 to 2.4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The low expression variants PolyA_6xΔ, INT1Δ373bp, and PROΔ225bp flowered as early as the deletion accession Nd-1.
source: Further, the low expression variants PolyA_6xΔ, INT1Δ373bp, and PROΔ225bp flowered as early as the deletion accession Nd-1 suggesting that there must be a critical lower threshold for FLM-ß to be effective (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: There must be a critical lower threshold for FLM-ß to be effective.
source: Further, the low expression variants PolyA_6xΔ, INT1Δ373bp, and PROΔ225bp flowered as early as the deletion accession Nd-1 suggesting that there must be a critical lower threshold for FLM-ß to be effective (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The correlation between FLM-δ and flowering time was much lower (R2 = 0.70) than for FLM-ß.
source: The correlation was much lower for FLM-δ (R2 = 0.70) suggesting that FLM-ß is the major determinant for flowering time in these conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FLM-ß is the major determinant for flowering time in the tested conditions.
source: The correlation was much lower for FLM-δ (R2 = 0.70) suggesting that FLM-ß is the major determinant for flowering time in these conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Temperature-sensitive FLM-ß regulation was significantly reduced in INT6+CAA between 15°C and 23°C when compared to the FLMCol-0 control variant (p=0.012).
source: When we statistically tested the interaction between genotype and temperature with a multiple linear model, we found that temperature-sensitive FLM-ß regulation was significantly reduced in INT6+CAA between 15°C and 23°C and when compared to the FLMCol-0 control variant (p=0.012) (Figures 4E and 6A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 4E and 6A,B.

claim: Flowering of the INT6+CAA variant was less sensitive to temperature changes when tested at 15°C and 23°C in homozygous T3 progeny plants and compared to the FLMCol-0 reference.
source: In line with the prediction, flowering of this variant was indeed less sensitive to temperature changes when tested at 15°C and 23°C in homozygous T3 progeny plants and compared to the FLMCol-0 reference (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Temperature-independent FLM-ß expression changes correlate with temperature-insensitive flowering in the selected temperature range.
source: Thus, temperature-independent FLM-ß expression changes correlate with temperature-insensitive flowering in the selected temperature range.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp variants showed similarly strong reductions of unprocessed pre-mRNA when compared to the levels of processed FLM mRNA.
source: When compared to the levels of processed FLM mRNA, the PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp variants showed similarly strong reductions of unprocessed pre-mRNA, suggesting that the respective deletion polymorphisms directly affect FLM transcription (Figures 4E,F and and 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E,F and 7A.

claim: The PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp deletion polymorphisms directly affect FLM transcription.
source: When compared to the levels of processed FLM mRNA, the PROΔ225bp and INT1Δ373bp variants showed similarly strong reductions of unprocessed pre-mRNA, suggesting that the respective deletion polymorphisms directly affect FLM transcription (Figures 4E,F and and 7A).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ lines had reduced FLM mRNA levels but did not show substantial changes in unprocessed pre-mRNA levels when compared to FLMCol-0.
source: In turn, the INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ lines had reduced FLM mRNA levels but, when compared to FLMCol-0, did not show substantial changes in unprocessed pre-mRNA levels (Figures 4E,F and and 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E,F and 7B.

claim: Post-transcriptional events may be affected in the INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ variants.
source: Since this indicated that post-transcriptional events may be affected in these variants, we tested for the abundance of differential polyadenylated splice variants after semi-quantitative 3'-RACE-PCR and sequencing of the cloned PCR products (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: A relative reduction of FLM-ß transcripts in INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ was accompanied by increases in the abundance of two polyadenylated transcripts containing exon 1 and intron 1 (E1I1p).
source: There, we detected a relative reduction of FLM-ß transcripts in INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ that was accompanied by increases in the abundance of two polyadenylated transcripts containing exon 1 and intron 1 (E1I1p) that had already been noted in an earlier publication (Figure 7C,D) (Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D and a citation to prior work.

claim: Not a single FLM-δ clone was identified among the 163 sequenced cDNAs.
source: Importantly, we did not identify a single FLM-δ clone among the 163 sequenced cDNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The relative increase in E1I1p transcripts could be independently confirmed by E1I1p-specific qRT-PCRs.
source: The relative increase in E1I1p transcripts could also be independently confirmed by E1I1p-specific qRT-PCRs and suggested in summary that splicing site choice at the exon 1 - intron 1 junction is changed in the INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ alleles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Splicing site choice at the exon 1 - intron 1 junction is changed in the INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ alleles.
source: The relative increase in E1I1p transcripts could also be independently confirmed by E1I1p-specific qRT-PCRs and suggested in summary that splicing site choice at the exon 1 - intron 1 junction is changed in the INT6+CAA and PolyA_6xΔ alleles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The nine PRO2+ and INT6+ haplotypes tested in transgenic experiments were present in 579 (69%) of all 840 accessions with available genome sequence information.
source: The nine PRO2+ and INT6+ haplotypes tested in transgenic experiments were present in 579 (69%) of all 840 accession with available genome sequence information (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The PRO2+/INT6+ haplotype significantly affected FLM-ß transcript levels.
source: We found that the PRO2+/INT6+ haplotype significantly affected FLM-ß transcript levels (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FLM-ß and FLC explained 32.9% (R2 = 0.329, p=0.0083) of flowering time variation in summer-annual accessions.
source: Using a multiple linear regression approach, we found that FLM-ß and FLC explained 32.9% (R2 = 0.329, p=0.0083) of flowering time variation, with FLM-ß significantly explaining a subfraction of 21.0% (R2 = 0.210, p=0.011) and FLC only 11.9%, however not significantly (R2 = 0.119, p>0.05) (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FLM-ß significantly explained 21.0% (R2 = 0.210, p=0.011) of flowering time variation in summer-annual accessions.
source: Using a multiple linear regression approach, we found that FLM-ß and FLC explained 32.9% (R2 = 0.329, p=0.0083) of flowering time variation, with FLM-ß significantly explaining a subfraction of 21.0% (R2 = 0.210, p=0.011) and FLC only 11.9%, however not significantly (R2 = 0.119, p>0.05) (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FLC explained only 11.9% of flowering time variation in summer-annual accessions, however not significantly (R2 = 0.119, p>0.05).
source: Using a multiple linear regression approach, we found that FLM-ß and FLC explained 32.9% (R2 = 0.329, p=0.0083) of flowering time variation, with FLM-ß significantly explaining a subfraction of 21.0% (R2 = 0.210, p=0.011) and FLC only 11.9%, however not significantly (R2 = 0.119, p>0.05) (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Flowering time responded stronger to FLM-ß levels in the accessions than in the transgenic variants (p=0.0321).
source: Further, by integration of expression data and flowering time data into a multiple linear model and comparison of the slopes, we found that flowering time responded stronger to FLM-ß levels in the accessions than in the transgenic variants (p=0.0321) (Figure 5B and Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 8.

claim: Variations in FLM-ß levels account for flowering time in cool ambient spring temperatures in a diverse population of summer-annual Arabidopsis accessions.
source: Taken together, we concluded that variations in FLM-ß levels account for flowering time in cool ambient spring temperatures in a diverse population of summer-annual Arabidopsis accessions (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: FLM-ß had a stronger effect in the control of flowering time than FLM-δ.
source: Our finding that FLM-ß had a stronger effect in the control of flowering time than FLM-δ indicates that previously phrased functional models proposing that FLM-δ had an antagonistic activity to FLM-ß need to be corrected (Posé et al., 2013; Sureshkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Previously phrased functional models proposing that FLM-δ had an antagonistic activity to FLM-ß need to be corrected.
source: Our finding that FLM-ß had a stronger effect in the control of flowering time than FLM-δ indicates that previously phrased functional models proposing that FLM-δ had an antagonistic activity to FLM-ß need to be corrected (Posé et al., 2013; Sureshkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FLM-δ levels are overall very low.
source: This is further supported by the fact that our results estimate that FLM-δ levels are overall very low and that we did not identify a single FLM-δ clone in a directed sequencing approach that identified 53 FLM-ß clones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The FLM-δ splice variant may be biologically irrelevant.
source: Our findings thus support more recent studies suggesting that the FLM-δ splice variant may be biologically irrelevant (Sureshkumar et al., 2016; Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: None of the amplification products detected with the primer combination used for FLM-δ has a biologically important function.
source: Our data thus support the conclusion that none of these amplification products has a biologically important function (Sureshkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: A twofold relative difference of FLM-ß levels was found when comparing the PRO2+GATAC and PRO2+AAACC variants with the lowest and highest FLM-ß expression, respectively.
source: A twofold relative difference of FLM-ß levels was found when comparing the PRO2+GATAC and PRO2+AAACC variants with the lowest and highest FLM-ß expression, respectively, and our linear model would predict a flowering time difference of 14.4 leaves at 15°C (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The linear model would predict a flowering time difference of 14.4 leaves at 15°C for the PRO2+GATAC and PRO2+AAACC variants.
source: A twofold relative difference of FLM-ß levels was found when comparing the PRO2+GATAC and PRO2+AAACC variants with the lowest and highest FLM-ß expression, respectively, and our linear model would predict a flowering time difference of 14.4 leaves at 15°C (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the linear model derived from experimental data.

claim: The PRO2+ region harbours a predicted MADS-box transcription factor binding site.
source: The PRO2+ region harbours a predicted MADS-box transcription factor binding site and several instances of auto- or cross-regulation of MADS-box factors have been described (de Folter et al., 2005; Kaufmann et al., 2009; Smaczniak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis.

claim: Several instances of auto- or cross-regulation of MADS-box factors have been described.
source: The PRO2+ region harbours a predicted MADS-box transcription factor binding site and several instances of auto- or cross-regulation of MADS-box factors have been described (de Folter et al., 2005; Kaufmann et al., 2009; Smaczniak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FLM expression may be regulated by MADS-box transcription factors and PRO2+ polymorphisms may modulate the efficiency or specificity of these binding events and thereby modulate basal FLM expression.
source: It can therefore be envisioned that FLM expression is regulated by MADS-box transcription factors and that PRO2+ polymorphisms modulate the efficiency or specificity of these binding events and thereby modulate basal FLM expression.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: The deletion of a 373 bp fragment in FLM intron 1 resulted in an elevenfold reduction in FLM expression and earlier flowering by 11.5 leaves as experimentally determined.
source: Similarly, the deletion of a 373 bp fragment in FLM intron 1 resulted in an elevenfold reduction in FLM expression and earlier flowering by 11.5 leaves as experimentally determined.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Intronic cis-regulatory transcription factor binding sites have been identified in other MADS-box transcription factors.
source: Intronic cis-regulatory transcription factor binding sites have been identified in other MADS-box transcription factors and interactions of enhancer and silencer elements that reside in the promoter sequence or the 3'-end of the first intron were reported (Hong et al., 2003; Schauer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Similar mechanisms may govern the expression of FLM at intron 1 sites that may act in isolation or together with binding events at the FLM promoter.
source: Thus, similar mechanisms may govern the expression of FLM at intron 1 sites that may act in isolation or together with binding events at the FLM promoter.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: Natural polymorphisms in intron 6 (INT6+) led to about fourfold differences in the abundance of FLM-ß.
source: Interestingly, natural polymorphisms in intron 6 (INT6+) led to about fourfold differences in the abundance of FLM-ß, which could, as predicted by the linear model, relate to a flowering time delay by 28.8 leaves, suggesting that INT6+ harbours extensive potential to fine-tune flowering (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: INT6+ polymorphisms could, as predicted by the linear model, relate to a flowering time delay by 28.8 leaves.
source: Interestingly, natural polymorphisms in intron 6 (INT6+) led to about fourfold differences in the abundance of FLM-ß, which could, as predicted by the linear model, relate to a flowering time delay by 28.8 leaves, suggesting that INT6+ harbours extensive potential to fine-tune flowering (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the linear model derived from experimental data.

claim: INT6+ harbours extensive potential to fine-tune flowering.
source: Interestingly, natural polymorphisms in intron 6 (INT6+) led to about fourfold differences in the abundance of FLM-ß, which could, as predicted by the linear model, relate to a flowering time delay by 28.8 leaves, suggesting that INT6+ harbours extensive potential to fine-tune flowering (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The INT6+CAA molecular effect appears to be mediated by effects on the splicing efficiency and specificity at the distal intron 1.
source: Importantly, this molecular effect appears to be mediated, in the case of INT6+CAA, by effects on the splicing efficiency and specificity at the distal intron 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: INT6+CAA promotes the formation of short intron 1-containing transcripts, at the expense of FLM-ß, that are likely subjected for degradation by nonsense-mediated decay.
source: There, INT6+CAA promotes the formation of short intron 1-containing transcripts, at the expense of FLM-ß, that are likely subjected for degradation by nonsense-mediated decay (Figure 7) (Lutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 7 and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The INT6+ site is directly flanked by a short PolyA motif.
source: The INT6+ site is directly flanked by a short PolyA motif and such sites represent potential recognition sites of hnRNP (heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein) splicing factors.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis.

claim: PolyA motifs represent potential recognition sites of hnRNP (heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein) splicing factors.
source: The INT6+ site is directly flanked by a short PolyA motif and such sites represent potential recognition sites of hnRNP (heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein) splicing factors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The predicted hnRNP binding pattern at INT6+ depended on the INT6+ haplotype, when predicted by web-based algorithms.
source: The predicted hnRNP binding pattern at INT6+ depended indeed on the INT6+ haplotype, when predicted by web-based algorithms, and their binding preference and activity, in concert with other splicing or transcriptional regulators, may ultimately be the basis of the splicing changes observed here (Piva et al., 2012; Carrillo Oesterreich et al., 2011; Reddy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by computational analysis.

claim: hnRNP binding preference and activity, in concert with other splicing or transcriptional regulators, may ultimately be the basis of the splicing changes observed.
source: The predicted hnRNP binding pattern at INT6+ depended indeed on the INT6+ haplotype, when predicted by web-based algorithms, and their binding preference and activity, in concert with other splicing or transcriptional regulators, may ultimately be the basis of the splicing changes observed here (Piva et al., 2012; Carrillo Oesterreich et al., 2011; Reddy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An extended PolyA motif, as it is present in the INT6+AAA variant when compared to the Col-0 reference variant INT6+AAT, correlated with strong increases in FLM-ß but not in FLM-δ abundance.
source: In support of this conclusion, we found that an extended PolyA motif, as it is present in the INT6+AAA variant when compared to the Col-0 reference variant INT6+AAT, correlated with strong increases in FLM-ß but not in FLM-δ abundance (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PolyA motifs are known to prevent nucleosome binding and changes of chromatin architecture may influence splicing.
source: PolyA motifs are known to prevent nucleosome binding and changes of chromatin architecture may influence splicing (Reddy et al., 2013; Suter et al., 2000; Wijnker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several hnRNPs have a reported role in flowering time regulation in Arabidopsis and wheat.
source: We noted with interest, however, that several hnRNPs have a reported role in flowering time regulation in Arabidopsis and wheat (Kippes et al., 2015; Fusaro et al., 2007; Streitner et al., 2012; Xiao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Residual FLC transcript may also slightly contribute to variation of flowering time of summer-annual accessions.
source: First, we showed that residual FLC transcript may also slightly contribute to variation of flowering time of summer-annual accessions, possibly interfering with the effects of FLM-ß (Balasubramanian et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Additional sequence variation in FLM in natural accessions may contribute to relevant expression changes.
source: Further, additional sequence variation in FLM in natural accessions may contribute to relevant expression changes, e.g. in the part of intron 1 identified as essential for FLM expression but not analysed in further detail here (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: It is possible that accessions harbour variation in the FLM-related MAF2 - 4, and this variation may differentially affect flowering time, in isolation or in combination with variation of their common interaction partner SVP.
source: Then, it is possible that these accessions harbour variation in the FLM-related MAF2 - 4, and this variation may differentially affect flowering time, in isolation or in combination with variation of their common interaction partner SVP (Ratcliffe et al., 2003; Airoldi et al., 2015; Scortecci et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The detected effect of FLM-ß on flowering (21%) in cool (15°C) temperatures is considerable and is rather an underestimation.
source: Bearing these possible genetic and environmental interferences in mind, we regard the detected effect of FLM-ß on flowering (21%) in cool (15°C) temperatures as considerable and suggest that it is rather an underestimation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and considerations of potential confounding factors.

claim: A uniform distribution of nine PRO2+/INT6+ haplotype combinations among the genetic clusters was found.
source: We found a uniform distribution of nine PRO2+/INT6+ haplotype combinations among the genetic clusters that have recently been established based on the analysis of genomic sequences from 1135 Arabidopsis accessions (The 1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis and a citation to recent literature.

claim: The PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT haplotype was overrepresented among the relict accessions.
source: Interestingly, the PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT haplotype was overrepresented among the relict accessions and the PRO2+AAAAC/INT6+AAA haplotype was overrepresented among the Asian group (The 1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and a citation to recent literature.

claim: The PRO2+AAAAC/INT6+AAA haplotype was overrepresented among the Asian group.
source: Interestingly, the PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT haplotype was overrepresented among the relict accessions and the PRO2+AAAAC/INT6+AAA haplotype was overrepresented among the Asian group (The 1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and a citation to recent literature.

claim: Both the PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT and PRO2+AAAAC/INT6+AAA haplotypes were associated with increased FLM-ß transcript levels and consequently late flowering.
source: In our experiments, both of these haplotypes were associated with increased FLM-ß transcript levels and consequently late flowering (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The relict and Asian accessions have been proposed to originate from glacial refugia from where central Europe was recolonized after the last ice age.
source: Since the relict and Asian accessions have been proposed to originate from glacial refugia from where central Europe was recolonized after the last ice age, these late-flowering PRO2+/INT6+ haplotypes may represent original haplotypes (Sharbel et al., 2000; Schmid et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The late-flowering PRO2+/INT6+ haplotypes may represent original haplotypes.
source: Since the relict and Asian accessions have been proposed to originate from glacial refugia from where central Europe was recolonized after the last ice age, these late-flowering PRO2+/INT6+ haplotypes may represent original haplotypes (Sharbel et al., 2000; Schmid et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The late flowering phenotype associated with the PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT and PRO2+AAAAC/INT6+AAA haplotypes would be in line with the hypothesis that late flowering alleles are more ancient and that early flowering alleles were derived only during the more recent Arabidopsis evolution.
source: The late flowering phenotype associated with these haplotypes would be in line with the hypothesis that late flowering alleles are more ancient and that early flowering alleles were derived only during the more recent Arabidopsis evolution (Toomajian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic linkage among the PRO2+ and INT6+ polymorphic sites was overall low (R2 = 0.11–0.55).
source: Further, genetic linkage among the PRO2+ and INT6+ polymorphic sites was overall low (R2 = 0.11–0.55) and the sequences surrounding PRO2+ and INT6+ were comparatively conserved.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis.

claim: The sequences surrounding PRO2+ and INT6+ were comparatively conserved.
source: Further, genetic linkage among the PRO2+ and INT6+ polymorphic sites was overall low (R2 = 0.11–0.55) and the sequences surrounding PRO2+ and INT6+ were comparatively conserved.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis.

claim: Mutations in the PRO2+ and INT6+ sites independently arose multiple times and these sites were preferentially selected during Arabidopsis flowering adaptation.
source: Taken together, this suggests that mutations in the PRO2+ and INT6+ sites independently arose multiple times and that these sites were preferentially selected during Arabidopsis flowering adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: All PRO2+/INT6+ alleles displayed a broad geographic distribution, except PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT, which was overrepresented in Spain.
source: All PRO2+/INT6+ alleles displayed a broad geographic distribution, except PRO2+GGAAC/INT6+AAT, which was overrepresented in Spain (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microclimates at specific geographic locations rather than general climate conditions at broad geographic regions may be important to drive adaptation of flowering to changing ambient temperature.
source: Likely, microclimates at specific geographic locations rather than general climate conditions at broad geographic regions may be important to drive adaptation of flowering to changing ambient temperature, as it was previously suggested for broadly distributed non-coding haplotypes of FLC that explain variation in vernalization (Li et al., 2014; Weigel, 2012; Shindo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in cis-regulatory regions are important for adaptation and phenotypic evolution and have a low probability to generate negative pleiotropic effects.
source: Mutations in cis-regulatory regions are important for adaptation and phenotypic evolution and have a low probability to generate negative pleiotropic effects (Swinnen et al., 2016; Meyer and Purugganan, 2013; Wray, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FLM may be an ideal candidate for flowering time adaptation through non-coding sequence variation at PRO2+ and INT6+ sites since changes in FLM-ß abundance precisely modulate flowering while maintaining phenotypic plasticity and without generating negative pleiotropic effects.
source: FLM may be an ideal candidate for flowering time adaptation through non-coding sequence variation at PRO2+ and INT6+ sites since changes in FLM-ß abundance precisely modulate flowering while maintaining phenotypic plasticity and without generating negative pleiotropic effects (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Changes at the PRO2+ and INT6+ sites should allow adapting flowering time in response to altered geographic distribution and consequently climate conditions as well as during changing global environments.
source: Changes at the PRO2+ and INT6+ sites should allow adapting flowering time in response to altered geographic distribution and consequently climate conditions as well as during changing global environments (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The role of FLM orthologues in other Brassicaceae, including a number of agronomically important species, is as yet not understood.
source: The role of FLM orthologues in other Brassicaceae, including a number of agronomically important species, is as yet not understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It is at present not possible to predict the role of Arabidopsis FLM polymorphisms for flowering time adaptation and plant breeding in the Brassicaceae family.
source: It is thus at present not possible to predict the role of Arabidopsis FLM polymorphisms for flowering time adaptation and plant breeding in this plant family.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: In view of the availability of new genome editing methodologies, the knowledge about important non-coding regions may be useful to fine-tune flowering time.
source: However, in view of the availability of new genome editing methodologies, the knowledge about important non-coding regions may be useful to fine-tune flowering time (Shan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential applications, supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Fine-tuning flowering time may allow buffering the anticipated negative effects on agricultural systems that occur as a consequence of small temperature changes during climate change.
source: This may allow buffering the anticipated negative effects on agricultural systems that occur as a consequence of small temperature changes during climate change (Moore and Lobell, 2015; Wheeler and von Braun, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential applications, supported by citations to prior literature.
